groups.title: Docker & Containerization
groups.question: Explain how you would package an API with Docker and run it locally next to its database.

followUps.Dockerfile — Layers, Multi-stage Builds: Why copy package.json and run npm install before copying the rest of the code?
followUps.Docker Compose — Local Multi-service Dev: What does Docker Compose do for an API that needs Postgres and Redis?

evidence.text: Each Dockerfile step makes a cached layer that Docker reuses if its inputs didn't change.
Copying package.json and installing first means code changes don't re-run the slow install.
Multi-stage builds and .dockerignore keep build tools and local node_modules out of the final image.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Dockerfile, layers) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the order of Dockerfile steps only affects readability.

evidence.text: One file defines the API, Postgres and Redis containers and starts them all with one command.
The services reach each other by name on a shared network, with their env vars and ports set.
Everyone gets the same versions and setup, closer to production.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Docker Compose) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says Compose merges all the services into one container.

groups.title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions
groups.question: Explain how you would make every pull request get checked automatically before it can be merged.

followUps.GitHub Actions — Workflow Syntax & Trigg: Which trigger runs a workflow on pull requests, and why isn't running only on main enough?
followUps.CI Pipeline — Lint, Test & Build Gates: Which checks belong in a CI pipeline, and what does blocking merges on them protect?

evidence.text: The pull_request trigger runs the workflow on every pull request.
Running only on main finds problems after they are merged; running on PRs catches them before.
The result shows on the pull request, so failures are seen before merging.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (GitHub Actions, pull_request) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says running on main is enough because reviewers check pull requests.

evidence.text: CI runs lint, tests and a build, such as the Docker image, on every pull request.
Merging is blocked until those checks pass.
So main always works and can be deployed, and any new failure is clearly new.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (CI, lint, tests) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says CI is only for deploying, not for checking code.

groups.title: Production Observability
groups.question: Explain how you would know what your API is doing in production, and how it should start and stop safely.

followUps.Structured Logging with Pino or Winston: Why log JSON objects instead of plain text lines?
followUps.Health Check Endpoints & Graceful Shutdo: What should happen to in-flight requests when the platform sends SIGTERM?

evidence.text: Each log line is a JSON object with fixed fields, like level, time, requestId, userId and message.
Log tools can filter and count by those fields, for example all errors for one user in the last hour.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Pino, Winston, JSON logs) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says JSON logs are mainly about making logs nicer to read.

evidence.text: On SIGTERM the server stops accepting new connections and starts failing its health check.
In-flight requests are allowed to finish, with a time limit.
Database pools and other resources are closed, then the process exits.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (SIGTERM, graceful shutdown, health check) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says in-flight requests are moved to another instance automatically.

groups.title: Deployment Platforms
groups.question: Explain how you would deploy an API to a managed platform and find out when it breaks.

followUps.Railway & Render — Zero-config Cloud Dep: What does a platform like Render handle for you that you would otherwise set up yourself?
followUps.Error Tracking with Sentry: What does Sentry give you about an error that a user's bug report doesn't?

evidence.text: It builds and deploys straight from your repo or Dockerfile.
It handles TLS certificates, restarting crashed processes, health checks, scaling and zero-downtime deploys.
It manages environment variables, secrets and networking.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Render, Railway, PaaS) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the platform fixes bugs and crashes in your own code.

evidence.text: Errors are captured automatically, including ones users never report.
Each comes with the stack trace, request data, user, release and breadcrumbs of what happened before.
Similar errors are grouped with counts, so you see how often it happens and who is affected.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Sentry, error tracking) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says Sentry fixes the errors automatically.
